Talk about the standards of behavior you expect in your group, and discuss the ways you typically discipline children in your care.<ref>http://www.today.com/parents/oh-behave-disciplining-other-people-s-kids-wbna30313559</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 2 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Create routines. When kids know what to expect every day, they’re less likely to misbehave. Establish a predictable schedule in your classroom or daycare. Give the kids a heads-up several minutes before you transition from one activity to the next.<ref>http://articles.extension.org/pages/25720/establishing-predictable-routines-in-a-child-care-setting</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 3 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Use incentives and reward systems. Encourage cooperation and good behavior by creating goals and rewards for the whole group. Measure progress in a way that’s easy for the kids to follow, like putting stickers on a chart or filling a jar with marbles.<ref>https://www.supernanny.co.uk/Advice/-/Parenting-Skills/-/Discipline-and-Reward/How-to-Discipline-Groups-of-Children.aspx</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 4 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Encourage good behavior. Notice when a child in your group does something thoughtful or kind. Give them a high-five or a few words of praise, and tell them why you’re proud of them. Positive reinforcement will make kids want to continue behaving well.<ref>http://lifehacker.com/six-tips-on-disciplining-children-from-an-experienced-t-1679048782</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 5 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Avoid using the word “don’t.” If it seems like the kids in your group aren’t listening to you, make sure you’re phrasing your instructions clearly enough. Tell them what you want them to do, not what you don’t want them to do. Otherwise, they may get confused.<ref>http://articles.extension.org/pages/25703/basic-tips-child-care-providers-can-use-to-guide-childrens-behavior</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 6 Version 5.jpg|center]]

#Separate misbehaving kids from the group. If a certain child is being disruptive to the group, ask them to come and sit or stand with you. Remain in a place where you can keep supervising the others.<ref>http://www.mass.gov/edu/docs/eec/licensing/technical-assistance/child-guidance-group-child-care-discipline.pdf</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 7 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Talk with the child about their behavior. In terms the child can understand, explain why their behavior wasn’t acceptable. Help them understand how their actions affect other people.<ref>https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/12/opinion/sunday/raising-a-moral-child.html?_r=0</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 8 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Address the behavior instead of the child’s character. Effective discipline involves teaching, not punishment. Avoid implying that the child is a bad person for misbehaving. Instead, tell them that you know they can do better, and help them think of more appropriate ways to act.<ref>https://afineparent.com/be-positive/positive-discipline.html</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 9 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Use consequences. Teach the kids in your group that actions have consequences. For disruptive behaviors like fighting, create some negative consequences, like missing recess. For positive behaviors like sharing, offer a few words of praise or a small treat like a sticker.<ref>https://www.empoweringparents.com/article/how-to-discipline-young-kids-effectively-4-steps-every-parent-can-take/#</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 10 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Make your consequences fair to the whole group. Don't let a few bad apples spoil the whole bunch. It's unfair to punish the entire group of kids if a few are acting up. In such cases, it may work to give the misbehaving kids an extra assignment to dissuade talking or playing. Other kids might work silently or go outside for recess.[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 11 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Avoid criticizing or blaming the children. It is always more effective to use positive reinforcement than to use negative punishment. Try not to blame the children or criticize them heavily, as they may begin to resent you or feel bad about themselves. Instead, reduce their privileges by using timeouts and restricting their playtime. This will teach them that their actions have consequences. [[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 12 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Be consistent. Know what your rules are, and stick to them. Don’t change your standards arbitrarily. If you aren’t consistent with your discipline, you’ll send the message that good behavior isn’t important all the time.<ref>https://psychcentral.com/lib/the-5-cs-of-effective-discipline-setting-rules-for-children/</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 13 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Model positive and kind interactions. Children learn more from your behavior than they do from your words. Show your group how you want them to act by using good manners, treating others with kindness, and being patient. In addition,  be cordial and positive when interacting with other teachers and administrators to model appropriate behavior.[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 14 Version 3.jpg|center]]

#Stay calm and collected. When a child acts up, don’t lose your temper with them, even if you’re frustrated.<ref>[v161711_b01]. 19 February 2021</ref> Speak in a low voice, and use calm movements. By keeping your cool, you’re modeling good conflict resolution skills while letting the child know you’re in control of the situation.<ref>https://www.supernanny.co.uk/Advice/-/Parenting-Skills/-/Discipline-and-Reward/How-to-stay-calm-with-your-child.aspx</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 15 Version 3.jpg|center]]

But if you’re a parent, childcare worker, or teacher, you’ll probably have to correct kids’ behavior in a group setting at some point, so it’s a good idea to learn how to handle this situation. Start by establishing clear expectations and good habits in your group, which can prevent disruptive behavior before it starts. After that, practice correcting misbehavior in a firm but compassionate way. Throughout it all, make sure you’re setting a good example with your own behavior.

added: Enforcing discipline in a group of children can be tricky. But if you’re a parent, childcare worker, or teacher, you’ll probably have to correct kids’ behavior in a group setting at some point, so it’s a good idea to learn how to handle this situation. Start by establishing clear expectations and good habits in your group, which can prevent disruptive behavior before it starts. After that, practice correcting misbehavior in a firm but compassionate way. Throughout it all, make sure you’re setting a good example with your own behavior.
[[Category:Behavioral Issues]]
==Steps==
===Establishing Good Habits===

#Have positive expectations. Show the kids in your group that you believe in them. Interact with them in a warm, friendly way, and get to know each of them as an individual. Look for the best in them, instead of waiting for a reason to discipline them.<ref>https://www.responsiveclassroom.org/want-positive-behavior-use-positive-language/</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 1 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*If you are a teacher, make every child feel like a valued member of the group by greeting them by name when they enter the classroom.

#*Put a positive spin on things. If one child is frequently boisterous, say something like, “Hannah, I’m glad you have so much energy today! Now let’s focus on doing our worksheets before we go outside.”

#Talk to the children’s parents. Make sure that you and the parents of the kids in your group are on the same page about discipline. Talk about the standards of behavior you expect in your group, and discuss the ways you typically discipline children in your care.<ref>http://www.today.com/parents/oh-behave-disciplining-other-people-s-kids-wbna30313559</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 2 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*You should ask the parents how they discipline their children at home. They may be able to provide suggestions that work well for their individual children.

#Create routines. When kids know what to expect every day, they’re less likely to misbehave. Establish a predictable schedule in your classroom or daycare. Give the kids a heads-up several minutes before you transition from one activity to the next.<ref>http://articles.extension.org/pages/25720/establishing-predictable-routines-in-a-child-care-setting</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 3 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*For instance, announce, “Okay, five more minutes on the playground, and then we’ll go back inside for story time.”
#*Make sure to balance hands-on activities with quiet activities in your schedule.

#Use incentives and reward systems. Encourage cooperation and good behavior by creating goals and rewards for the whole group. Measure progress in a way that’s easy for the kids to follow, like putting stickers on a chart or filling a jar with marbles.<ref>https://www.supernanny.co.uk/Advice/-/Parenting-Skills/-/Discipline-and-Reward/How-to-Discipline-Groups-of-Children.aspx</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 4 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*For instance, you could let each child put a marble in the jar when they finish reading a book by themselves. When the jar is full, take the whole group on an outing to the library.

#Encourage good behavior. Notice when a child in your group does something thoughtful or kind. Give them a high-five or a few words of praise, and tell them why you’re proud of them. Positive reinforcement will make kids want to continue behaving well.<ref>http://lifehacker.com/six-tips-on-disciplining-children-from-an-experienced-t-1679048782</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 5 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*For example, say, “Jesse, it was nice of you to share your candy with the other kids. I’m proud of you for being so generous.”
===Correcting Negative Behaviors===

#Avoid using the word “don’t.” If it seems like the kids in your group aren’t listening to you, make sure you’re phrasing your instructions clearly enough. Tell them what you want them to do, not what you don’t want them to do. Otherwise, they may get confused.<ref>http://articles.extension.org/pages/25703/basic-tips-child-care-providers-can-use-to-guide-childrens-behavior</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 6 Version 3.jpg|center]]
#*For instance, say, “Savannah, can you use your indoor voice, please?” instead of “Savannah, don’t talk so loudly.”

#Separate misbehaving kids from the group. If a certain child is being disruptive to the group, ask them to come and sit or stand with you. Remain in a place where you can keep supervising the others.<ref>http://www.mass.gov/edu/docs/eec/licensing/technical-assistance/child-guidance-group-child-care-discipline.pdf</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 7.jpg|center]]
#*If two or more children start fighting, have all of them come over with you. Separate them so they can’t keep fighting.
#*If the disruptive child is upset or angry, give them some time to cool down. Ask them to sit quietly, or read them a book until they’re calmer.

#Talk with the child about their behavior. In terms the child can understand, explain why their behavior wasn’t acceptable. Help them understand how their actions affect other people.<ref>https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/12/opinion/sunday/raising-a-moral-child.html?_r=0</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 8.jpg|center]]
#*For instance, you could say something like, “Do you remember how you felt last week when Jill took your markers without asking? That’s how Michael felt when you took his toys today.”
#*Take the child’s age into account as you talk to them. Younger children may need multiple reminders before they understand why certain behaviors are wrong.
#*Talk to the child privately if you can, and discipline them separately away from the group. Don’t lecture them about misbehaving in front of the rest of the group.

#Address the behavior instead of the child’s character. Effective discipline involves teaching, not punishment. Avoid implying that the child is a bad person for misbehaving. Instead, tell them that you know they can do better, and help them think of more appropriate ways to act.<ref>https://afineparent.com/be-positive/positive-discipline.html</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 9.jpg|center]]

#*For instance, don’t say, “Why are you being such a bad boy?” or “Why can’t you behave?” Instead, say, “It’s not okay to hit other people, because that hurts them. Let’s think of some better ways to tell people you’re mad at them.”

#Use consequences. Teach the kids in your group that actions have consequences. For disruptive behaviors like fighting, create some negative consequences, like missing recess. For positive behaviors like sharing, offer a few words of praise or a small treat like a sticker.<ref>https://www.empoweringparents.com/article/how-to-discipline-young-kids-effectively-4-steps-every-parent-can-take/#</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 10.jpg|center]]

#Make your consequences fair to the whole group. Don't let a few bad apples spoil the whole bunch. It's unfair to punish the entire group of kids if a few are acting up. In such cases, it may work to give the misbehaving kids an extra assignment to dissuade talking or playing. Other kids might work silently or go outside for recess.[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 11.jpg|center]]

#*When misbehaving kids see others getting free time or special treats, they are more likely to clean up their acts. If the other kids don't get any special treatment, there's no motivation to behave well.

#*Constantly calling out a single child or solely blaming them for misbehavior can make the child feel isolated from the rest of the children. They may start thinking that they do not fit in, and it may create resentment.

#Avoid criticizing or blaming the children. It is always more effective to use positive reinforcement than to use negative punishment. Try not to blame the children or criticize them heavily, as they may begin to resent you or feel bad about themselves. Instead, reduce their privileges by using timeouts and restricting their playtime. This will teach them that their actions have consequences. [[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 12.jpg|center]]
===Setting a Good Example===

#Be consistent. Know what your rules are, and stick to them. Don’t change your standards arbitrarily. If you aren’t consistent with your discipline, you’ll send the message that good behavior isn’t important all the time.<ref>https://psychcentral.com/lib/the-5-cs-of-effective-discipline-setting-rules-for-children/</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 13.jpg|center]]
#*Sometimes you might need to change your rules or make an exception. When this happens, give your group a clear explanation of what’s happening and why. Otherwise, the kids may be confused.

#Model positive and kind interactions. Children learn more from your behavior than they do from your words. Show your group how you want them to act by using good manners, treating others with kindness, and being patient. In addition,  be cordial and positive when interacting with other teachers and administrators to model appropriate behavior.[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 14.jpg|center]]
#*For instance, always say please and thank you, whether you’re interacting with children or adults.

#Stay calm and collected. When a child acts up, don’t lose your temper with them, even if you’re frustrated. Speak in a low voice, and use calm movements. By keeping your cool, you’re modeling good conflict resolution skills while letting the child know you’re in control of the situation.<ref>https://www.supernanny.co.uk/Advice/-/Parenting-Skills/-/Discipline-and-Reward/How-to-stay-calm-with-your-child.aspx</ref>[[Image:Discipline a Group of Children Step 15.jpg|center]]
#*Losing your temper might get kids to behave temporarily, but it also sends the message that you aren’t really in charge.
#*If you need to, pause and take a deep breath to compose yourself before dealing with a misbehaving child.

added: Enforcing discipline in a group of children can be tricky. But if you’re a parent, childcare worker, or teacher, you’ll probably have to correct kids’ behavior in a group setting at some point, so it’s a good idea to learn how to handle this situation. Start by establishing clear expectations and good habits in your group, which can prevent disruptive behavior before it starts. After that, practice correcting misbehavior in a firm but compassionate way. Throughout it all, make sure you’re setting a good example with your own behavior.
[[Category:Behavioral Issues]]
==Steps==
===Establishing Good Habits===

#Have positive expectations. Show the kids in your group that you believe in them. Interact with them in a warm, friendly way, and get to know each of them as an individual. Look for the best in them, instead of waiting for a reason to discipline them.<ref>https://www.responsiveclassroom.org/want-positive-behavior-use-positive-language/</ref>
#*If you are a teacher, make every child feel like a valued member of the group by greeting them by name when they enter the classroom.

#*Put a positive spin on things. If one child is frequently boisterous, say something like, “Hannah, I’m glad you have so much energy today! Now let’s focus on doing our worksheets before we go outside.”

#Talk to the children’s parents. Make sure that you and the parents of the kids in your group are on the same page about discipline. Talk about the standards of behavior you expect in your group, and discuss the ways you typically discipline children in your care.<ref>http://www.today.com/parents/oh-behave-disciplining-other-people-s-kids-wbna30313559</ref>

#Create routines. When kids know what to expect every day, they’re less likely to misbehave. Establish a predictable schedule in your classroom or daycare. Give the kids a heads-up several minutes before you transition from one activity to the next.<ref>http://articles.extension.org/pages/25720/establishing-predictable-routines-in-a-child-care-setting</ref>
#*For instance, announce, “Okay, five more minutes on the playground, and then we’ll go back inside for story time.”
#*Make sure to balance hands-on activities with quiet activities in your schedule.

#Use incentives and reward systems. Encourage cooperation and good behavior by creating goals and rewards for the whole group. Measure progress in a way that’s easy for the kids to follow, like putting stickers on a chart or filling a jar with marbles.<ref>https://www.supernanny.co.uk/Advice/-/Parenting-Skills/-/Discipline-and-Reward/How-to-Discipline-Groups-of-Children.aspx</ref>
#*For instance, you could let each child put a marble in the jar when they finish reading a book by themselves. When the jar is full, take the whole group on an outing to the library.

#Encourage good behavior. Notice when a child in your group does something thoughtful or kind. Give them a high-five or a few words of praise, and tell them why you’re proud of them. Positive reinforcement will make kids want to continue behaving well.<ref>http://lifehacker.com/six-tips-on-disciplining-children-from-an-experienced-t-1679048782</ref>
#*For example, say, “Jesse, it was nice of you to share your candy with the other kids. I’m proud of you for being so generous.”
===Correcting Negative Behaviors===

#Avoid using the word “don’t.” If it seems like the kids in your group aren’t listening to you, make sure you’re phrasing your instructions clearly enough. Tell them what you want them to do, not what you don’t want them to do. Otherwise, they may get confused.<ref>http://articles.extension.org/pages/25703/basic-tips-child-care-providers-can-use-to-guide-childrens-behavior</ref>
#*For instance, say, “Savannah, can you use your indoor voice, please?” instead of “Savannah, don’t talk so loudly.”

#Separate misbehaving kids from the group. If a certain child is being disruptive to the group, ask them to come and sit or stand with you. Remain in a place where you can keep supervising the others.<ref>http://www.mass.gov/edu/docs/eec/licensing/technical-assistance/child-guidance-group-child-care-discipline.pdf</ref>
#*If two or more children start fighting, have all of them come over with you. Separate them so they can’t keep fighting.
#*If the disruptive child is upset or angry, give them some time to cool down. Ask them to sit quietly, or read them a book until they’re calmer.

#Talk with the child about their behavior. In terms the child can understand, explain why their behavior wasn’t acceptable. Help them understand how their actions affect other people.<ref>https://www.nytimes.com/2014/04/12/opinion/sunday/raising-a-moral-child.html?_r=0</ref>
#*For instance, you could say something like, “Do you remember how you felt last week when Jill took your markers without asking? That’s how Michael felt when you took his toys today.”
#*Take the child’s age into account as you talk to them. Younger children may need multiple reminders before they understand why certain behaviors are wrong.
#*Talk to the child privately if you can. Don’t lecture them about misbehaving in front of the rest of the group.

#Address the behavior instead of the child’s character. Effective discipline involves teaching, not punishment. Avoid implying that the child is a bad person for misbehaving. Instead, tell them that you know they can do better, and help them think of more appropriate ways to act.<ref>https://afineparent.com/be-positive/positive-discipline.html</ref>

#*For instance, don’t say, “Why are you being such a bad boy?” or “Why can’t you behave?” Instead, say, “It’s not okay to hit other people, because that hurts them. Let’s think of some better ways to tell people you’re mad at them.”

#Use consequences. Teach the kids in your group that actions have consequences. For disruptive behaviors like fighting, create some negative consequences, like missing recess. For positive behaviors like sharing, offer a few words of praise or a small treat like a sticker.<ref>https://www.empoweringparents.com/article/how-to-discipline-young-kids-effectively-4-steps-every-parent-can-take/#</ref>
===Setting a Good Example===

#Be consistent. Know what your rules are, and stick to them. Don’t change your standards arbitrarily. If you aren’t consistent with your discipline, you’ll send the message that good behavior isn’t important all the time.<ref>https://psychcentral.com/lib/the-5-cs-of-effective-discipline-setting-rules-for-children/</ref>
#*Sometimes you might need to change your rules or make an exception. When this happens, give your group a clear explanation of what’s happening and why. Otherwise, the kids may be confused.

#Be positive and kind. Children learn more from your behavior than they do from your words. Show your group how you want them to act by using good manners, treating others with kindness, and being patient.<ref>http://www.webmd.com/parenting/family-health-12/how-to-child-discipline?page=3</ref>
#*For instance, always say please and thank you, whether you’re interacting with children or adults.

#Stay calm and collected. When a child acts up, don’t lose your temper with them, even if you’re frustrated. Speak in a low voice, and use calm movements. By keeping your cool, you’re modeling good conflict resolution skills while letting the child know you’re in control of the situation.<ref>https://www.supernanny.co.uk/Advice/-/Parenting-Skills/-/Discipline-and-Reward/How-to-stay-calm-with-your-child.aspx</ref>
#*Losing your temper might get kids to behave temporarily, but it also sends the message that you aren’t really in charge.
#*If you need to, pause and take a deep breath to compose yourself before dealing with a misbehaving child.
